title: Prime-length necklaces
pages: A readout is the clockwise sequence of bead colors from a marked start. A ring identifies readouts that differ by rotation only. Reflections are not identified: keep rings face up. A ring with n positions can have fewer than n distinct readouts when its coloring repeats.

Period divides length. The number d of distinct readouts is the smallest positive rotation that restores the coloring, and d divides n. Equivalently the ring consists of n/d repeats of a block of length d. Constant rings have d=1. For prime length p, the only possible values are 1 and p; every ring using at least two colors has p distinct readouts.

Counting and Fermat. With c≥1 colors and p prime, there are cp marked readouts, of which c are constant. The remaining cp-c readouts partition into rotation families of size p. Thus p divides cp-c, and the number of rings is c+(cp-c)/p. This is the divisibility form of Fermat’s little theorem, with a concrete counting proof.

Limits. Do not divide all readouts by the ring length: constant and periodic rings have smaller families. For a composite length, a mixed ring can repeat early; the prime formula need not count correctly. The congruence for a particular color count is not a converse primality test.

K-1: Make rings, match by turning, and compare the number of different starts on small examples. Recognizing A/B, counting to 6 and moving a start arrow are enough. Physical sorting and a complete short case list are genuine mathematical outcomes.

Grades 2-3: Partition the supplied cards for lengths 3 and 5, contrast a length-4 early repeat, and conjecture or explain why mixed five-bead rings have five views. Counting to 32 and equal-sized grouping are useful; reading all cards aloud is unnecessary.

Grades 4-5: Prove the prime-length orbit claim, count rings with three or c colors, and derive divisibility. Product counting and division are needed for the final formula. A class that establishes only the length-5 case has not yet proved the prime-length theorem.

Five pair-kits of six A and six B counters, printed ring templates, and a movable paper start arrow. Use flat face-up mats rather than jewelry that can flip. Print one extra eight-card page per table and one 32-card page for each older table; older children can cut the card rectangles themselves. A no-cut option is to mark each family in one color on the supplied sheet. Add a third counter color only for upper P6.

Returning children may recognize rotation from Week 4. The new destination is equal-sized families at prime length and their divisibility consequence, not a new claim about rotation itself. Unpiloted.

0-6 minutes: Let children place counters on a three-position mat. Use the printed AAB example: keep the ring fixed and move the start clockwise, obtaining AAB, ABA, BAA. These are three readouts of one ring. Show AAA as a different ring. Keep reading clockwise and never turn the mat face down.

6-23: Work on the three-bead rings and eight-card sort. 23-28: Stand, bring a ring to another pair and ask whether it matches theirs by turning. 28-48: Compare the four-bead case, or sort five-bead cards cooperatively. 48-60: Share a group-size claim and its explanation. K can remain with four positions; upper pupils can take the prime argument only after they own the smaller examples.
Three-bead key: K P1-2; middle and upper P1-2

There are four rings, with family sizes 1,3,3,1. The group sizes are not all the same. All eight words are accounted for, so the list is complete. Dividing 8 by 3 would wrongly treat AAA and BBB as three-card families. The correct count is 2+(8-2)/3=4.
P3. Exactly two rings have two As and two Bs: AABB (the As adjacent) and ABAB (the As opposite). Each pair of A positions is either adjacent or opposite, exhausting the possibilities.

P4. One readout: AAAA or BBBB. Two: ABAB, with readouts ABAB and BABA. Four: AAAB, with AAAB,AABA,ABAA,BAAA; AABB and ABBB also work. Exactly three is impossible; a return must fit evenly into four positions (proof on page 4).

P5. Exactly two rings: AABBB and ABABB. The two A beads are adjacent or separated, up to turning; on five positions there is only one nonadjacent separation. Each has five different readouts. AABBB gives AABBB,ABBBA,BBBAA,BBAAB,BAABB; ABABB gives ABABB,BABBA,ABBAB,BBABA,BABAB.

P6. Examples using both colors: ABABAB has two readouts; AABAAB has three; AAAAAB has six. The first repeats AB, the second repeats AAB, and the last has one B whose six positions distinguish all starts. No exhaustive list of six-bead rings is requested.

P3. The possible numbers are 1,2,4, with examples AAAA, ABAB, AAAB. Three is impossible. A repeating block must fit an integer number of times around the ring; the block-length proof is on page 4. A physical alternative: a match after three steps forces the same color all around the four-position cycle, so it was a one-readout ring already.
P4. There are eight five-bead rings: two singleton families and six families of five. These are the exact groups for the printed 32 cards, whose numbering is in alphabetical order.
Card numbers in its rotation family

P5. No mixed five-bead ring can have fewer than five readouts. If a rotation by 1,2,3 or 4 places restores the ring, repeatedly moving by that amount visits all five positions. All those positions must carry the same color, contradicting the ring being mixed. For an accessible demonstration, label positions 0-4: steps of 2 visit 0,2,4,1,3,0; steps of 3 reverse that order. Steps of 1 or 4 also visit every position.
P6. The two constant words do not belong to five-card families, so 32/5 is invalid. Count them separately: 2+(32-2)/5=2+6=8.

If children count a ring twice, keep one mat fixed and turn the other through every position. If a family has a repeated card, ask whether the whole readout changed, not merely the arrow. For completeness, sort by the number of A beads. For the 32-card page, assign different first-two-letter branches to pairs, then merge rotation matches. Give the cards rather than ask a child to manufacture all 32 words.
When a child says “every mixed ring has as many views as beads,” test ABAB before revealing the prime rule. This makes the hypothesis earn its place.

P3. Sizes 1,2,4 are possible; size 3 is not. The six length-4 rings are represented by AAAA,BBBB (size 1), ABAB (size 2), and AAAB,AABB,ABBB (size 4). A repeated shorter block, here AB twice, lets a mixed ring return early.

P4. Use the complete 32-card key on page 3. The result is eight rings: two of size 1 and six of size 5. Four admits a nonconstant block of length 2 repeated twice; five has no proper divisor except 1, whose block would be constant.

P5. Exactly p distinct readouts for a prime-length p ring using at least two colors. If rotation by k positions, 0<k<p, restored the coloring, the positions 0,k,2k,... modulo p would all have the same color. These visit all p positions: a repetition before p steps would give p dividing mk for 0<m<p, impossible since p is prime. The ring would be constant. Thus every nonzero rotation changes it and all p starts differ.

P6. With three colors and length 5, there are 35=243 readouts. Three are constant; the other 240 form 48 families of five. Total: 51 rings. Generally the count is c+(cp-c)/p, because each of the p positions independently has c choices. The nonconstant readouts partition into families of p, proving p divides cp-c.
Why the smallest period divides the length

Let d be the least positive rotation that restores an n-position ring; n itself always does. Write n=qd+r with 0≤r<d. A rotation by qd restores it, and so does a full turn n; consequently their difference r also restores it. Minimality forces r=0, so d divides n. Starts separated by d give the same word; starts with different remainders modulo d cannot agree, or a smaller positive difference would restore the ring. Hence there are exactly d distinct readouts.

This is the missing justification behind “the block must fit.” It proves the composite obstruction as well as the prime case. A child’s complete physical sort proves the particular finite count; the period argument explains why the count generalizes.
Optional extension: why face up matters

Compare the six-bead rings AABABB and AABBAB. They match after a reflection but not by rotation. The rotations of AABABB are AABABB, ABABBA, BABBAA, ABBAAB, BBAABA, BAABAB; none is AABBAB. This gives a small concrete reason that allowing flips would change the objects being counted.
